turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Denise, come through. Sharon, grab the chair by the window. What's brought you in?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's this cough, and I'll try to keep it short, though I never do. Dry and tickly, back of the throat, worse when I lie down, and a sip of water helps for a minute. I reckon it's the tail of a cold, nothing more.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been at it six weeks, worse at night, up half the night. I hear her from the front room.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six is too long. I thought three weeks when I rang, but it was after Lorne, so four weeks. And I'm not up half the night. I wake once, have a sip, and I'm off again.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dry cough, four weeks on your reckoning, six on Sharon's, worse lying down, you blame a cold. Is there any phlegm?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all, dry as a bone. The aloe tissues are still in the packet, four dollars I won't get back.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fever? Shivers, feeling hot?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Chemist thermometer yesterday said 36.4, normal for me. Runny nose and sore throat from the cold are finished, but I couldn't tell you the date that cold began.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gone completely, those two?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Completely. Barley sugar for the throat, not real medicine, and the nose just dried up on its own.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's puffed on the back stairs. She stops halfway.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not puffed. Coles yesterday, two bags, no trouble. It's coughing, not breathlessness, Sharon just worries.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You stopped halfway on Tuesday. I was behind you with the washing.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped to cough, not to get my breath. The milk was heavy, that's a different story.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any wheeze, or chest pain with the cough?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No wheeze, no chest pain. A sip of water eases the tickle for a minute, then it comes back.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about heartburn, or a sour taste?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really, no. One curry on Saturday caught me, and that was the curry. I don't get reflux.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the blood pressure. How long have you had that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was sixty-two. I'm seventy-one, so nine years, and it's still there. That's the other thing I wanted to mention, not just the cough.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you actually taking for it?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): They put me on enalapril, no, ramipril, I mix those two up every time. Two and a half milligrams, no, ignore that, the bottle says five milligrams, once a day.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She started the ramipril five weeks ago, after the last appointment. I still reckon it's the tablet doing it, not a cold.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The cough is the cold, Sharon, not the tablet. I take the ramipril every morning, I don't miss that one, and I take it with the water tablet.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the water tablet, in your words.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the indapamide, two point five milligrams, mornings, for the pressure. Little white one. I've called it the water tablet for years, and the chemist on High Street knows exactly what I mean.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She missed the water tablet twice last week. They were still sitting in the dosette on Thursday and Sunday.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Those were spare Panadol, the little white ones look the same if the light's poor. I take the indapamide every single morning. I line them up on the saucer so I can see them.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): So ramipril five milligrams daily, new five weeks ago, and indapamide two point five, which you say you never skip. Anything else you take?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol, the odd one, if the knee niggles, not every day. And that's me. My brother Kevin is on lisinopril, not me. He coughed for months and they changed him, and Sharon brings it up every time we have tea.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Kevin's lisinopril stays off your list, it's his. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I can pretty much take what's put in front of me.
[SEG0033] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The sulphur tablets. She came out in a rash years ago, when the old GP tried them for a water infection.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't reckon that was an allergy. I had a gastro at the same time, and I've had Bactrim since with no drama. I wouldn't put allergy on my form.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): All right. You don't accept an allergy, Sharon remembers a rash with a sulphur drug, so I'll leave it unclear, not definite. High blood pressure in the family?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Kevin's got it, and Dad had it too. Mum didn't, she had the sugar, but that's not me and I won't wander off into Mum's story.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoking? Alcohol?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked, not a single cigarette. A glass of sav blanc with dinner a few nights a week, and that's the limit. My sister Sharon lives in the front room, so I'm not rattling around the house alone.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The wine I'll vouch for. It's the stairs, and whether she should still be doing that morning walk down to the river.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll check the pressure while we talk. 152 over 90, and the pulse is 74. Did you take a home reading?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): This morning I thought it said one-sixty over ninety-five, but I had the digits wrong. It was 146 over 84. I wrote it on the pad. The pulse was 70-something, I didn't bother keeping it.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen. Chest is clear, no wheeze, no crackles. Throat's not inflamed. Ankles aren't puffy.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): There you go, breathing's fine. My neighbour had a cough for a month after a cold, which proves nothing, I know, but it feels the same.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to call this an ACE-inhibitor cough. It might be the ramipril, it might be the tail of that virus, and reflux can give a dry cough even without heartburn. I can't separate those today, so there's no firm diagnosis, and the clear chest doesn't settle it either. We'll just note the length as somewhere between four and six weeks.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're not saying it is the tablet.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not concluding that. I am going to stop the ramipril, and tomorrow morning you start candesartan, eight milligrams, once a day, in its place. Keep taking the indapamide exactly as you are.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Do we bin the ramipril, then?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't bin it, and don't take any more of it. Bring the box next visit so the chemist record matches. If your lips or tongue swell, if you become properly breathless, or if you cough up blood, go to emergency, don't wait for me.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Lips or tongue, properly breathless, blood, emergency. And the candesartan is instead of the ramipril, not on top of it. I'll say it twice so I don't muddle the dosette.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Instead, not on top. I'm not ordering a chest x-ray today. If the cough hasn't eased when I see you next, then I'll arrange one.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): When is next? Thursday mornings suit me. Arvos don't, Sharon's at the pool and I won't get a lift.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): In three weeks. We'll recheck the pressure and see what the cough is doing. Still no firm label on it until we've watched it off the ramipril.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll book at the desk. And the morning walk, is that off?
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): The walk can stay. No need to stop it on account of this.

[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Three weeks, candesartan eight instead of ramipril five, water tablet stays, walk stays. And the glass of wine is still allowed, or have you quietly cancelled that?
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): The wine, as you described it, is fine. Keep a note of the cough and the morning readings on that pad.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll write them under the 146. And I'll tell the chemist, when I pick up the candesartan, not to pack the ramipril again. I do talk their ear off, they know me.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good plan. Sharon can grab that three-week appointment on the way out, and we'll take it from there.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

omissions.text: Negative finding asked and answered: no shivers/feeling hot with the cough.
Patient denied sour taste as well as heartburn/reflux symptoms ('Not really, no... I don't get reflux').
Medication timing detail: patient takes ramipril every morning.
Home pulse was reported as '70-something' but not recorded.
Doctor explicitly said no firm diagnosis and would not call this an ACE-inhibitor cough at this stage.
Doctor stated they are not ordering a chest x-ray today.
Follow-up purpose/detail: in three weeks they will recheck blood pressure and reassess what the cough is doing.
Real disagreement about cause: caregiver thinks ramipril is causing the cough, while patient thinks it is the tail of a cold; doctor does not conclude either way.
Plan detail: patient was advised to tell the chemist not to pack ramipril again when picking up candesartan.
